stories.title_en: A Secretly Stamped Mark Wins the Bedding

paragraphs.en: In the country there was a man known as You the Shyster, who flouted the law, was a relentless litigant, and preyed on ordinary folk. Word of his shifty ways spread, and everyone feared him and kept their distance. One day he went to the prefectural city by boat and was the first aboard, already seated. The later passengers came crowding in — strangers thrown together by chance, none knowing any of the others — and they sat facing one another in the boat, chatting idly. The talk happened to turn to the touring censor's arrests of litigious troublemakers. Among them was a young man surnamed Qiu, who did not know You the Shyster was on the boat. He said to the group: “I hear that in our county these days You Wu is the worst shyster of all. No one who spends even a short time around him escapes being cheated and hurt. If the touring censor would only get rid of the man, the people could live in peace.” You Wu laughed coldly to himself: “What is it to you, that you trumpet my shiftiness and even wish the censor would be rid of me? If I don't swindle this fellow out of something for nothing, my name as a shyster is wasted on me.” Noticing that young Qiu's bedding roll was a fine one, he took out a wooden seal, edged up to a light patch on the felt wrapping, and secretly stamped a mark on it.

In the evening the boat reached the shore, and each man gathered his luggage and left. You the Shyster trailed along behind young Qiu. When they reached the front of the prefectural offices, he snatched the bedding from the servant's carrying pole, saying: “Much obliged for the carrying — I'll take it from here.” Young Qiu lunged to grab it back: “That's my bedding — where do you think you're taking it?” The two of them grappled, neither giving way, until the quarrel carried them right into the prefectural court. You said: “It's mine — he's trying to force a claim.” Qiu said: “He's seizing my property.” The prefect said: “You both claim it. What identifying mark does each of you have?” Qiu said: “I bought it myself and made no mark.” You said: “I stamped a seal inside the felt.” They opened it up right there in court; You took the wooden seal from his sash and matched it to the mark, and sure enough they were the same. The prefect said: “This is You's property. How dare Qiu falsely claim it!” He had Qiu given ten strokes of the bamboo, ordered You to take the bedding away, and drove them both out of the yamen. Qiu cursed him: “Who are you, you thief, that you dare cheat me like this? I will pay you back for this!” You Wu said: “That ‘You the Shyster’ you were talking about on the boat — that's me. What was it to you, going on all day about how shifty I am? So I taught you a lesson: this is how a shyster operates.” Only then did Qiu feel regret: “I spoke ill of a man recklessly, and so brought this loss on myself.”

Note: Who does not hate a vicious shyster? But if you do not know the man, do not lightly broadcast his faults. He may be listening at your elbow, and he will nurse the hatred in his heart. Then, the moment you show a weakness, he will seize the opening and poison you — and you will not even know where it came from. That is why the ancients thrice sealed their mouths and were careful with their words. Lord Pang's way of leaving his descendants peace was simply to speak well of everyone. You Wu was wicked, no doubt; but why did young Qiu gossip about him behind his back and bring on You Wu's brazen seizure of his bedding? That is a far cry from Lord Pang's way of leaving peace behind him. So Confucius hated those who proclaim other people's faults, and Mencius warned against speaking of others' failings — both are the sages' way of teaching us to keep clear of resentment. One cannot be too careful with words.

stories.title_en: A Plaster over the Eyes, an Ingot Snatched

paragraphs.en: In the county town there was a silversmith whose family was fairly well off. The tax forwarders who collected the autumn grain-tax silver often entrusted him with melting it down. One day he was melting silver ingots, and, feeling there were still spots inside that had not fused through, he boiled and washed them again that night. His shop door had a wide crack in it, and from outside one could see in. A crook bought a large medicinal plaster and crept up in the night to peek. He watched the man finish washing two ingots and set them by the furnace. Then the crook, outside, began to groan in pain and cried: “Open the door!” The silversmith asked: “Who is it?” The crook answered from outside: “I've been badly beaten by a thieving brute. I beg you, let me warm a plaster at your furnace so I can put it on.” The silversmith opened the door and let him in. The crook limped along, hands trembling, groaning in pain, his hair a tangled mess, head bowed. He warmed the large plaster at the furnace until it softened, then slapped it with both hands straight onto the silversmith's face, snatched one ingot, and ran. The burning pain was more than the silversmith could stand; he tore the plaster off in a frenzy, but the ingot was already gone with the thief. He shouted “Thief!” and rushed out in pursuit, but had no idea which way the man had gone. After a few dozen paces of chasing at a loss, he could only go back, bitter and heartsick.

Note: This crook's act — groaning in pain, begging to be let in, warming a plaster at the furnace — was truly hard to see through. But an ingot is a weighty thing; had he put it away first and only then opened the door, there would have been no loss. Let those who come after take note: anyone carrying silver must never lightly let a suspicious stranger get close.

stories.title_en: Lime in the Eyes to Snatch the Silver

paragraphs.en: Sun Tao was a man of Henan. He regularly bought cotton cloth and sold it in Jianning Prefecture in Fujian. One night he was melting silver at the shop of Wang Liu the silversmith. The melting was done, and two packets of silver sat on the table. The two men were still checking the silver when a thief walked straight into the shop and flung lime into their eyes. The two had their hands full saving their eyes, and the thief simply took the packets of silver from the table and walked off. Tao chased after him for dear life. He had nearly caught him when the thief dropped one packet on the ground. Tao picked up the packet and went back; when he opened it at the silversmith's shop, it was all iron. And in the end there was no trail to catch him by.

Note: As the saying goes, “A thief is a petty man, but his wits outrun a gentleman's.” How true that is. When he first came into the shop, he flung lime to burn their eyes, leaving them no time to look to their money; when the chase had nearly caught up with him, he dropped a packet on the ground — that stopped the pursuit and got him clear. Was this just a case of the thief biding his time to perfection, and of careless keeping inviting theft? Still, Tao's own habitual carelessness had brought it about. Be warned by this, as a man once choked grows careful with his food — that is the lesson to take away.

stories.title_en: Robbed by Crooks in Broad Daylight While Relieving Himself

paragraphs.en: Wang Heng was a man of Yangzhou Prefecture in the Nanjing region, a clerk in the prefectural office. His two terms of service were complete, and he was due to go up to the capital to be processed for a post. His family was poor and he had no funds, so he scraped together a loan of ten-odd taels of silver from relatives and friends and set out alone for Beijing, to cover the costs of the appointment. He had just arrived in the capital and was relieving himself on the grass by the drill ground. No sooner had he pulled his trousers down than two crooks seized him, cursing him as they pulled at his clothes: “You thief — you stole our clothes!” Then and there they grabbed his clothes together with his silver and ran off. By the time he got up, tied his trousers, and gave chase, the two crooks were already far away. Heng had been on the road for many days and his strength was spent; though he chased for dear life, he could not catch them. Choked with regret and rage, he had no choice but to beg a loan of travel money at the Huitong government hostel and head home, to make other arrangements later.

Note: A lone traveler away from home must guard against robbery not only in out-of-the-way places. Even when relieving himself on a main road, he should take his trousers right off and keep them tucked under his arm. Then, if some smooth operator means mischief, he can get up and run, or stand and fight. Wang Heng knew no such caution, and the crooks took his clothes and his silver, every last bit of them. At that point, with no travel money to be found, what became of his prospects? Had his fellow clerks at the Huitong Hostel not lent him the money for the journey back, he would have ended up little better than a beggar.
